meta.title: Who really said "Surround yourself with people who make you happy. People who make you laugh, who help you when you're in need. People who genuinely care. They are the ones worth keeping in your life. Everyone else is just passing through"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Wikiquote lists this exact line under Misattributed for Karl Marx. No work of his contains it, and the rival same-name-composer story is itself unsourced.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Surround yourself with people who make you happy. People who make you laugh, who help you when you're in need. People who genuinely care. They are the ones worth keeping in your life. Everyone else is just passing through'?
meta.ogDescription: Not the philosopher. Wikiquote files this wording under Misattributed — and the popular 'it was a composer named Karl Marx' fix is unsourced too.

answer.label: Not Karl Marx — an unsourced modern aphorism
answer.authorDates: Origin undocumented · circulating under Marx's name by 2013
answer.sourceLine: No work of Karl Marx contains this sentence, and English Wikiquote lists this exact wording in the Misattributed section of its Karl Marx page. The popular correction — that it belongs to a German composer who happened to share the name — is no better sourced than the error it replaces: nobody has produced a book, letter, interview or recording from either man. What can be documented is only where the sentence has been seen, not where it came from.
answer.confidenceText: Disputed — no source exists for either claimant

source.heading: Where the trail runs out
source.excerpt: Surround yourself with people who make you happy. People who make you laugh, who help you when you're in need. People who genuinely care. They are the ones worth keeping in your life. Everyone else is just passing through.
trail: English Wikiquote files this exact sentence in the Misattributed section of its Karl Marx page ↗, where the only explanation offered is that it belongs to a composer of the same name. No work, edition or date accompanies it — because none has ever been produced.

That entry is not old scholarship. It was added on 9 February 2014 by an anonymous editor in a single edit ↗ that supplied both the quotation and the composer explanation at once, citing nothing for either.

The sentence was loose under the philosopher’s name before Wikiquote caught up with it: an archived Goodreads page from 6 April 2013 ↗ already credits it to Karl Marx, author of The Communist Manifesto, with no book named.

Quote Investigator, which has traced several lines wrongly given to Marx, has no article on this one at all — so there is no deeper research behind the composer claim waiting to be found. The place to test any line claimed as Marx’s remains the Marx/Engels Archive of his collected works ↗.
source.cutTag: No work. No page. No edition.
source.excerptNote: There is no fuller context to show, and that absence is the finding. A genuine quotation can be widened — the sentence before it, the page it sits on, the edition it was printed in. This one cannot be widened at all: it appears fully formed on quotation sites and nowhere else, with no chapter, no first printing and no named writer behind it.
source.rightsNote: No rights status can honestly be asserted for this wording. Public-domain status attaches to a work with a known author and a known first publication, and this sentence has neither — no located source, no edition, no identifiable writer. Karl Marx’s own writings have long been out of copyright, but that is beside the point here, because this line is not among them; and if it were in fact written by someone living in the modern era, it could well still be in copyright to an author nobody has yet named.

author.name: Karl Marx
author.heading: About the man on the graphic
author.bio: Karl Marx was born in Trier in the Kingdom of Prussia in 1818 and died in London in 1883, having spent most of his adult life stateless and in exile. He wrote as a philosopher and political economist — The Communist Manifesto with Friedrich Engels in 1848, then the three volumes of Das Kapital — and his subject was the machinery of production, class and history, not the management of one’s social circle. His writing about human relations sits in the register of alienation and labour; the vocabulary of ‘people who genuinely care’ and ‘worth keeping in your life’ belongs to a much later idiom, one that postdates him by well over a century.

misattribution.heading: Two Karl Marxes, no source
misattribution.intro: Karl Marx is one of the internet’s most dependable magnets for lines he never wrote, and this is among the odder cases — because the popular correction is as undocumented as the mistake it claims to fix.

items.why: English Wikiquote places this exact wording in the Misattributed section of its Karl Marx page ↗ — not Disputed, not Sourced. No book, essay, letter, article or speech of his has ever been offered for it, and the aggregator pages that carry it name no work either.

Wikiquote’s only explanation is that the line belongs to a composer of the same name, but the entry cites nothing, and the composer’s own biography ↗ records a catalogue of choral and instrumental music — Rilke settings, a viola concerto, a passacaglia — and nothing resembling an English aphorism. Treating this as the answer swaps one unsupported name for another.

The composer story did not start here. It was first attached to the separate ‘There comes a time in your life…’ passage — still published that way by PassItOn, crediting ‘Karl Marx Composer’ ↗ — while Goodreads files that text under the memoirist José N. Harris ↗. Two different sentences, one borrowed explanation.

misattribution.truthLine: The safe answer is the unglamorous one: this sentence has no located author. It is wrong to call it Marx’s, and unsupported to call it the composer’s — Wikiquote records the misattribution ↗, but nobody has yet documented the origin.

context.heading: A fake with a fake correction
lead: Most misattributions are simple: a good line drifts toward a famous name and sticks. This one is stranger, because it arrived with its own debunking already attached — and the debunking is as thin as the claim. Ask the internet who really said it and you will be told, confidently, that it was ‘the other Karl Marx, the composer.’ That answer has been repeated for well over a decade without anyone ever pointing to a page, a programme note, a letter or an interview in which the composer said anything of the kind.

Follow the composer story back and it does not even lead to this sentence. It was first attached to a different passage of circulating text — the one beginning ‘There comes a time in your life when you have to let go of all the pointless drama’ — and only later slid across onto this one, carrying its air of authority with it. Two unsourced quotations, one unsourced explanation, shared between them.
context.detailsSummary: Why ‘it was the composer’ is not an answer
detailsBody: Karl Marx (1897–1985) was a real person: a German composer and music teacher whose published catalogue runs to choral works, settings of Rilke, a viola concerto and a passacaglia. What he did not leave, so far as any catalogue or reference work shows, is a body of English-language aphorisms about choosing your friends.

The mechanism is easy to see once you look at it. A quotation is challenged; someone offers a name-twin as the explanation; the explanation is satisfying, requires no evidence, and is far more repeatable than ‘we do not know.’ It then gets written into a reference work, and from there it is quoted back as though it had been established. The honest position is duller and firmer: this sentence has no known author, and pinning it on a second Karl Marx does not change that.
context.pull: The correction is not a source. It is a second guess wearing the costume of research.

sourcesVerified.claim: English Wikiquote's Karl Marx page lists this exact wording in its Misattributed section, with the note that it is attributed to a composer of the same name, and cites no work or source.

The Misattributed entry for this quote was added to Wikiquote on 9 February 2014 (revision 1679961) by an anonymous IP editor, supplying both the quotation and the composer note in a single edit with no source cited.

Karl Marx the composer lived 12 November 1897 to 8 May 1985, was a German composer and music teacher, and his works include settings of Rainer Maria Rilke, a Viola Concerto Op. 10 and a Passacaglia Op. 19; the article records no aphorism of the 'surround yourself' kind.

Karl Marx the philosopher was born 5 May 1818 in Trier, Kingdom of Prussia, died 14 March 1883, and is described as a German philosopher, social and political theorist and revolutionary socialist; his works include The Communist Manifesto (1848) and Das Kapital (1867-1894).
Goodreads credits this exact quote to Karl Marx with no book or source cited, shows 674 likes, and states that quotes are added by the community and are not verified by Goodreads.

As of the archived snapshot of 6 April 2013, Goodreads already carried this exact wording credited to Karl Marx (linked to the author page for the author of The Communist Manifesto), with no source named.
PassItOn publishes the separate text 'There comes a time in your life when you have to let go of all the pointless drama...' attributed to 'Karl Marx Composer'.
Goodreads credits the 'There comes a time in your life, when you walk away from all the drama and people who create it...' text to Jose N. Harris, not to Karl Marx.

A blog post published under a September 2011 date asserts that 'Karl Marx, the composer (not the philosopher)' said the 'There comes a time in your life...' text, and cites no source for that attribution.
Quote Investigator's own site search for this phrase returns no article about it; the only result returned is an unrelated article on a different quotation.
The Marxists Internet Archive hosts a gateway to Marx's selected and collected works, correspondence, biographical material and date/subject indexes.
